items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: when I was with his group we rehearsed without anything.

ctx.x: That’s fascinating, really. Was it a challenge then to, you started delving into oriental music and themes and so forth, to transfer that to this big band format?

Yes. I think that first of all — excuse me — I would like to think my big band is a real — it’s an extension of a small group, that’s the way I like to think. But there are many things that happen because of the first band, what they could do and so on and so on, I utilize them, blah blah blah blah. But when — as I say before — I decided at least I should try that. I was very fascinated by a Japanese drum called kotsuzumi, because my late father was a student of Noh, N-O-H, a man’s performing art, he was a…

that’s the best way to learn music I think. So some of the music was like a little bended a certain way, and I think that’s also very common in Japanese music, many notes are bended. The artistry of the Japanese instrumental music, it’s another skill but to change the shape of one note. That’s the artistry, and that includes bending a note also, so on and so on. So I think it becomes more like a color, a little bit different I think.

items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Charles Mingus, when later on I was with his group, and we used to rehearse [at] his apartment

ctx.x: Okay, Toshiko-san, I wanted for you to, um, as much as possible to describe that process, since you were classically trained as a pianist, and you heard Teddy Wilson, and so, Teddy Wilson is improvising, so what is it … how did you acquire the ability to improvise?

By taking all [of it] from records. [It] took me a long time to take it, because I didn‟t have that quick [an] ear. And many times, you know, play it, and then take it on the sheet music, and then I tried to play that, as many as I could. That is the way I learned, mainly, the jazz language. Also, the different tunes, you know, different…. Because there wasn‟t anything, books, or anything like that in those days. Interesting

thing is, like—I said Mister Fukui, I told you about, so I was there [Beppu], and then I moved to Fukuoka and I was in the officers‟ club, and I did the same thing, listen to records and take out, now… and I tried to play it on piano. And that‟s how I learned. Meanwhile, Mister Fukui sent me the book, How to Play Jazz Piano [possibly Modern Piano Method, 1933], it was a piano kyōsoku hon [method book], you know, like a lesson book, written by Vincent López. I‟d never heard [of him] before. And as … you have to…
